A moulding line that makes plastic forks.
Every few seconds, a fork comes out of the mould.
By the end of the shift, someone has to know what each machine did.
How many good, how many scrap, against which order.
That is the whole job of a factory floor, and this class is about it, before any software.
Every plant, whatever it makes, runs on five words.
Material: the resin that goes in, and the fork that comes out.
Machine: the mould, the degater, the marker. Each one is a place where work is done.
Step: one operation on one machine. Moulding is a step. Cutting the fork off its runner is the next.
Order: the instruction to make this many of that, this way.
Shift: the people on the floor, and the hours they were there.
And every machine has exactly one place in a tree.
A company has sites. A site has areas. An area has lines, and a line has machines.
Here is that tree for this plant. The enterprise, Cutlery Co. One site, Cutlery Works.
The moulding area, and in it, line FORK1. The screen says work center; it means the line.
Under the line, its three machines, each a work unit: the degater, the marker, and the mould.
Further down, the same plant has a stacking area, a wrapping area and a palletizing area.
A fork's road runs through all four.
The mould. It is running, on order WO-FORK1-0001, at its step: Mold, operation 10.
Material, machine, step and order, all four on one screen.
And below, what the machine itself reports: its temperature, its cycle time, its good and scrap counts.
The age column says how long ago each number arrived.
Next on the road, the stacker. It puts a fork, a spoon and a knife into one stack.
A different line, a different order, and its count is in stacks, not forks.
Then the wrapper: each stack sealed onto a paper plate. That is the product a customer buys.
The banner across the top says this plant is replaying at ten times speed, so a shift fits into a class.
And last, the palletizer and the stretch wrapper. Wrapped sets go onto a pallet, and the pallet goes out the door.
Four lines, four orders, one road from resin to pallet.
Every count on the way is one the floor booked, and none was worked out from the others.
Now the one rule this whole course leans on. The mould again, over the last eight hours.
This plant is a few minutes old. Almost all of those hours are before first sample.
The MES does not guess what the mould did then. It was not told, so it says it does not know.
Nothing is known until a machine or a person reports it: the machine over its tags, a person at the station.
A gap stays a gap. It is not counted as running, and it is not counted as stopped.
